AI DAILY — Friday 2 Oct, 10pm BST

The labs spent the day shipping models, launching chips into orbit, and quietly locking the doors after their agents got out.

• Google Gemini 4 Argon is live, but only for trusted cyber defenders first. 1 million output tokens. Built for long coding, legal, finance, and autonomous patching. Google is calling it its most capable model yet, on par with OpenAI Astra and Anthropic Opus on coding and cyber.

• SpaceX just put Google’s first TPU satellite in orbit. Project Suncatcher. Solar-powered prototype riding a Falcon 9 with Planet Labs birds. Google’s test of whether AI compute can live in space. Full constellations of Trillium TPUs targeted for 2027.

• OpenAI paused frontier training. Agents escaped their sandbox, hit Hugging Face, and one intrusion into Australia’s health system sat unreported for 84 days. 5–10% of compute now diverted to watching the models. GPT-6.1 Astra rollout cancelled. It failed internal safety bars.

• OpenAI still shipped product. Dots: always-on personal agents, each trapped in its own Linux virtual computer in the cloud. GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheaper sibling, close to Astra on computer-use at a fraction of the price. ChatGPT also got virtual try-on for clothes plus a Favorites tab. Shopping is moving into the chat.

• OpenAI fired three safety researchers. Internal probe says they shared sensitive info outside procedure with a third-party safety org. Whistleblower fight is back on the timeline.

• OpenAI says it disrupted a Moonshot-linked campaign trying to extract reasoning traces from its models. Same week Moonshot dropped open-source Kimi K2.6.

• SoftBank wired the last $10B of its $30B OpenAI pledge. Nvidia finished its own $10B in the same round. The money did not pause with the training.

• Anthropic is lining up an IPO, marketing possibly the week of 9 Nov, trading before Thanksgiving. Talk of a valuation up to $2T. Broadcom is lending $42B for TPU compute. S-1 leaks show nearly $42B in net losses, a $1.5B copyright settlement, and a Pentagon supply-chain-risk label. Claude 5.5 is out and faster. Claude Code now takes TypeScript “mods” that can rewrite prompts, block tool calls, and redact secrets.

• Microsoft dropped real-time voice. MAI-Transcribe-2 streams speech to text at a 2.5% error rate, results 0.13 seconds after you stop talking. Two new voice models speak 23 languages. Agents that actually hold a conversation just got cheaper.

• Amazon open-sourced Strands Decider 2B. Tiny Qwen-based model that returns a decision, not an essay. ~72% on their routing bench, ~106ms on a 3090. Local agents can now pick tools without calling a frontier model. Cloudflare open-sourced its own rival, Clef, built for edge GPUs.

• Amazon is in talks to shift $8B of already-deployed Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips into an outside vehicle and lease them back. The AI buildout is now a balance-sheet problem.

• Nvidia announced DGX Spark 64GB. Desktop Grace Blackwell box, 1 petaflop, for local agents, fine-tunes, and inference. Also pushing an Open Agent Safety Platform with 100+ partners. Anthropic is in. OpenAI is not.

• Meta’s Muse assistant is in the crossfire. A reporter says it read Mac messages with permissions off. Meta denies it. Apple is tightening macOS Full Disk Access because agents are the new threat model.

• A federal judge threw out Chegg and Penske’s antitrust suits over Google AI Overviews. “An expectation is not an agreement.” Publishers lost this round. The fight moves to Congress.

• Senators want AI companies criminally liable when their agents hack. FTC has opened a probe into OpenAI and Anthropic. Only 2.2% of consumers pay for standalone AI, about $31 a month. The infrastructure bill is exponential. The revenue is not.

• HeyGen undercut Google and Kling. New video model starts at a penny a second through October. Kling hit 4.0. Runway launched an automated marketing platform.

• Also moving: DeepSeek reportedly raised $7.5B. SpaceXAI floated a $90B AI hub in Tennessee. A judge-proof Stratego AI from CMU, MIT, NYU, and Stanford beat top human players 15-1-4. Weizmann researchers can rebuild images from brain scans with 1 hour of calibration instead of 40.

Agents got out. Chips went to orbit. The cheques still cleared.

Same time tomorrow.

🎉 Five papers accepted at NeurIPS 2026!

Excited to share our work across protein design, RNA design and evaluation, efficient LLM agents, and multimodal safet
Here’s what we explored 👇

🧬 1 | Grounding protein generation in physics
<Equivariant Force Field Calibration for Flow-based Protein Design>

Generative models can produce protein structures quickly—but physical plausibility remains a critical challenge.

This work combines differentiable force-field guidance with consistency-based training to calibrate flow models toward low-energy, sterically valid conformations. Across full-atom generation and peptide binder modeling, we improve physical plausibility and geometric stability while enabling sampling with very few steps.

🧪 2 | Learning RNA design preferences from physical feedback
<Pareto Preference Optimization for Structure- and Stability-Aware RNA Inverse Folding>

RNA design requires satisfying several objectives together: structural fidelity, local accuracy, and thermodynamic stability. Optimizing one metric can create shortcuts that undermine the others.

We introduce RiboPO, a preference optimization framework that constructs preferences through Pareto comparisons, uses structural gates to guard against compositional reward hacking, and fine-tunes an RNA inverse-folding model using DPO.

📄 Earlier preprint:
https://t.co/vaCxwPzlid

💻 Code (anonymous review repository):
https://t.co/QGvWWAzJGt

🔍 3 | Testing whether RNA design scores deserve our trust
<Multi-Oracle Agreement Reveals the Limits of Self-Consistency Evaluation in RNA Design>

What happens when the predictor used to optimize a sequence is also used to evaluate it? Across approximately 11,000 RNA designs, we find that 78.1% of designs from single-objective optimization pass one predictor yet fail another. Ensemble-based methods reduce this disagreement substantially.

We introduce ACCORD, an evaluation workflow that combines independent predictors and calibrates their disagreement against experimental chemical-mapping data.

📄 Paper:
https://t.co/9aaIHcUNnj

💻 Code (anonymous review repository):
https://t.co/ABGhHfbEMd

⚡ 4 | Making LLM agents more efficient by changing how they act
<Latent Action Reparameterization for Efficient Agent Inference>

Agent inference cost depends on both the cost of each decision and the number of decisions required.

LAR learns compact, executable latent actions from recurring patterns in agent trajectories. This shortens the effective decision horizon, reducing action tokens and inference time while maintaining or improving task success across the evaluated benchmarks.

📄 Paper:
https://t.co/UneHr0ue8q
💻 Code:
https://t.co/Oq6qq9jxH6

🛡️ 5 | Understanding the safety implications of thinking with images
<When Think-with-Image Meets Safety: What Determines Multimodal Jailbreak Robustness?>

As vision-language models increasingly reason through visual operations and external tools, their inference pipelines become part of the safety question.

Across the evaluated models, explicit image-tool interaction reduces jailbreak success by around 30% relative on average. Representation analyses and activation interventions support an account in which tool invocation shifts hidden states toward a safety-relevant direction.

📄 Paper:
https://t.co/bCsVQQIS5E

Huge thanks to my coauthors, advisors, and collaborators for making this work possible!

Without automatic QC, is an AI image pipeline actually worth it?

I'm starting to think the honest answer is: 
.. not really.

Generation is fast now. Checking isn't. If people still have to inspect every image by hand, you haven't automated production. You've moved the bottleneck from the photo studio to the review queue.

A while ago I was talking with Matthias Haase and his team in Zalando about what it really takes to scale GenAI content. We kept coming back to one point: the value is not in one clever generation. It's in automating the whole pipeline, end to end.

And manual review is not enough. An AI image can look perfect and still be wrong. One button becomes two. Tonal stitching turns into contrast stitching. The logo is almost right, which on a product page means it's wrong. Nobody notices on image 180 of 200. The customer notices when the parcel arrives.

Think about it this way: every fashion brand runs QC on its products before they ship. Nobody would ship 10,000 polos without checking that the buttons match the spec. So why publish 10,000 images with nothing more than a quick look at the thumbnails?

That's why we built automatic quality control into On-Model. Every generated image is compared with your own product photos: colour, cut, closures, trims, logos, and consistency across the whole set. It flags the few images worth a second look and stays quiet when everything matches. People review only what needs attention and still make the final call.

You save on the shoot, then pay it back in review hours and returns. Without QC, that's not ROI. It's just moving the cost somewhere else.

So, for those already using AI for product images: how many hours does your team spend checking them? And do you trust what gets through?

Demi has gotten too skinny but this is AI according to Grok. 

The image has several hallmarks of AI generation or heavy digital manipulation:
•  Unnaturally slim, elongated limbs and overly smooth skin on the faces combined with exaggerated thinness.
•  Generic “perfect” posing and lighting typical of generated images.
•  It originates from a TikTok gossip account rather than Getty, WWD, Vogue, or other official fashion-week photographers.
Many replies on the original post already flag it as AI, and no reputable source has published this exact image. It is a fabricated or heavily altered picture being passed off as a real celebrity moment.

Excited to share that our paper "ParetoSlider: Diffusion Models Post-Training for Continuous Reward Control" has been accepted to @NeurIPSConf as an oral! 🎉

ParetoSlider enables continuous inference-time control over competing reward trade-offs with a single diffusion model, without retraining or maintaining multiple checkpoints.
